opus-5.5.text:
I think it's useful to break "doing AI research" into its components, because it isn't one skill. There's coming up with a question worth asking, designing an experiment that actually tests it, writing and debugging the code, running it at scale, reading the results honestly, and then deciding what to do next. Right now, models are getting quite good at the middle pieces. Writing code, running experiments, even doing a first pass at analysis: a lot of that is already partially automatable, and it's improving very fast.

The hard parts are at the two ends. One end is taste: knowing which problem matters, which direction is likely to be fruitful, and which result is actually surprising versus just noise. The other end is long-horizon coherence. A real research project isn't a ten-minute task. It's weeks or months of accumulating context, hitting dead ends, revising your hypothesis, and remembering why you made a decision three weeks ago. Current agents still struggle to keep that thread over very long trajectories without drifting or fooling themselves.

So I see the progression roughly as: first, models become very strong research assistants that can execute well-specified experiments end to end. Then they start proposing their own variations and ablations within a direction a human sets. The last step, where the model itself picks the direction and judges what's important, is the one I'm least certain about in timing. But I don't think there's a fundamental wall there. Taste is learned from feedback, and if we can build environments where models get signal on whether their research choices were good, that can be trained too.

One thing I'd emphasize is evaluation. In math or coding you can verify an answer. In research, "was this a good idea?" often isn't clear for a long time. Figuring out how to give models reliable feedback on open-ended research is, to me, one of the central bottlenecks, and maybe more important than raw model capability at this point.

And honestly, AI research is a special case because it's self-referential. If models can meaningfully accelerate AI research, that feeds back into building better models. That's why so many people in the field care about this particular milestone. It's not just another benchmark. It could change the pace of everything after it.

r001.rationale: The response separates current, partial automation that can accelerate research from the later stage where a model chooses its own direction and judges what matters.

r002.rationale: It describes reading experimental results and deciding what to do next, including revising hypotheses over the course of a project.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that we're already partway there, and the remaining gap is less about raw intelligence than about something I'd call the loop.

Let me break the research task down. There's generating ideas, there's turning an idea into an experiment, there's running the experiment and debugging it when it inevitably breaks, there's reading the results and deciding what to do next, and then there's writing it up and arguing for it. If you look at those pieces individually, models are honestly decent at most of them right now. They can propose plausible ideas. They can write training code. They can read a loss curve. The part that's still weak is stringing those together over weeks, where each decision depends on everything that came before, and where the feedback is slow and noisy.

When I was working on things like ReAct and later on agents more broadly, the pattern I kept seeing was that the hard part wasn't the individual step. It was that errors compound. A small mistake in setting up the baseline means every conclusion downstream is wrong, and the agent doesn't notice because it has no ground truth to check against. A human researcher has this uneasy feeling of "something's off," and that intuition is built from years of being wrong. Models haven't had that many reps on long-horizon tasks yet, because we mostly trained them on short ones.

So my view on progression is that it's going to be driven by environments more than by model size. If you want a model to do a full research project, you need it to practice doing full research projects, with real compute, real failures, and reward signals that come from whether the thing actually worked. That's expensive and slow, which is why it's the bottleneck. But once you have that kind of training loop, I think progress will be fast, because research itself is quite verifiable compared to a lot of tasks. Did the number go up or not.

The other piece is taste. Which problems are worth working on. I used to think that was the truly human part, but I'm less sure now. A lot of taste is just having seen what works and what doesn't across many attempts, and models can see more attempts than any person. What they lack is skin in the game. They don't care if the project fails. Whether you can build that in artificially, or whether it even matters, I genuinely don't know yet.

If you ask me for a timeline, I'd say in the next couple of years we'll see agents reliably run the middle of the pipeline end to end, from a reasonably specified idea to a result and a draft. The two ends, picking the problem and knowing when a result is actually interesting rather than just positive, those will take longer, and I suspect they'll be the last things to go.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts capable individual research steps with completing a full project, but does not distinguish AI accelerating its own development from autonomously completing an AI research task.

r002.rationale: It describes reading experimental results and deciding what to do next, with later decisions depending on earlier steps.

astra-6.text:
I think the key distinction is between doing a step in research and owning the whole research process. You can ask a model to write some code, run an experiment, or analyze a result. But an entire research task requires it to decide what question matters, formulate a hypothesis, design experiments, and then revise its approach when the results are unexpected.

That last part is particularly important. Research is not a fixed sequence of instructions. Often, an experiment fails, and you have to figure out whether the idea is wrong, the implementation has a bug, or the experiment simply doesn’t distinguish between your hypotheses. An agent needs to make those decisions over a long period without constantly handing control back to a human.

So I would expect progress to happen first on more bounded tasks, where the objective is clear and feedback is relatively cheap. A human might supply the research question, and the AI handles implementation and experimentation. As those systems become more reliable, we can give them more responsibility for choosing the experiments and eventually for choosing the questions themselves.

The thing I would look for is whether the system can produce a useful, reproducible finding with less human intervention—not just whether it can generate something that looks like a paper.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes handling individual research steps from owning an entire research task, but it does not say that AI is already accelerating its own development.

r002.rationale: It describes analyzing unexpected experimental outcomes and revising an approach, but does not clearly state that this analysis informs hypotheses for subsequent experiments.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it helps to distinguish between doing individual research steps and owning the whole research process. An AI might already help you implement an idea, run an experiment, or analyze results. But an entire research task also involves deciding what question is worth asking, choosing what evidence would answer it, and changing direction when the experiments don’t support your hypothesis.

The difficult part is that research doesn’t give you a clean reward signal. If an experiment fails, is the idea wrong, is there a bug, or did you choose the wrong experimental setup? You have to make decisions under that uncertainty, sometimes over a long period of time.

So I expect progress to be gradual. We’ll first see agents complete relatively well-defined projects where humans provide the question, the environment, and the evaluation criteria. Then humans will delegate more of the experimental design and eventually more of the problem selection. The key milestone, to me, is whether the system can reliably turn an ambiguous goal into a useful result, including recognizing when its own approach isn’t working. That requires more than generating a plausible research plan—it requires learning from what actually happens.

r001.rationale: It contrasts AI helping with individual research steps against owning the whole research process, but does not distinguish accelerating AI’s own development from autonomously completing an AI research task.

r002.rationale: It says researchers analyze results, change direction when experiments contradict a hypothesis, and learn from what happens, communicating a results-driven loop that guides later research.
